In this paper, we introduce X-Nav, a novel framework for end-to-end cross-embodiment navigation where a single unified policy can be deployed across various Deep Reinforcement embodiments for both wheeled and quadrupedal robots. X-Nav Learning consists of two learning stages: 1) multiple expert policies are trained using deep reinforcement learning with privileged observations on a wide range of randomly generated robot embodiments; and 2) a single general policy is distilled from the expert policies via navigation action chunking with transformer Imitation Learning (Nav-ACT). The general policy directly maps visual and Deploymenton Unseen Commercially Available Robots proprioceptive observations to low-level control commands, General Policy enabling generalization to novel robot embodiments. Simulated experiments demonstrated that X-Nav achieved zero-shot transfer Transformer to both unseen embodiments and photorealistic environments. JSON: Name: x_nav Title: End-to-end cross-embodiment navigation via multi-expert DRL and transformer-based policy distillation Short Hypothesis: Distilling multiple privileged-observation deep reinforcement learning expert policies trained on randomly generated robot embodiments into a single transformer-based policy using navigation action chunking increases zero-shot navigation success rate and path efficiency on unseen wheeled and quadrupedal robots compared to policies trained on single embodiments or via offline behavioral cloning. Related Work: Existing approaches to generalizable robot navigation fall into two families. Imitation-learning methods train a single policy from heterogeneous datasets collected on multiple robots and commonly predict intermediate waypoints or velocities; they typically rely on embodiment-specific controllers or tracking modules and therefore suffer from compounding errors, require per-robot tuning, and have limited zero-shot transfer to robots with different dynamics or body sizes. Deep reinforcement learning approaches either use hierarchical architectures combining high-level planners with dynamics-aware low-level controllers or monolithic policies trained on one embodiment; these methods often require embodiment-specific dynamics models, trajectory trackers, or velocity planners and do not simultaneously handle diverse robot morphologies and low-level executable commands. Recent transformer- and diffusion-based decoders improve expressive power for action generation but still depend on intermediate controllers or narrow training distributions. Open limitations include dependence on embodiment-specific modules, lack of end-to-end low-level command generalization across robot types, sensitivity to robot size/dynamics mismatch, and limited evidence of scalable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Abstract: We present a two-stage research pipeline for end-to-end cross-embodiment navigation where a single unified policy executes low-level control on unseen wheeled and quadrupedal robots. Stage one trains multiple expert policies with privileged observations using deep reinforcement learning on a large set of randomly generated robot embodiments and varied terrain types. Stage two distills the ensemble of experts into one general policy via transformer-based navigation action chunking and imitation learning, producing temporally coherent, low-level action sequences directly from onboard depth and proprioceptive inputs. The main contribution is a scalable distillation architecture that encodes multi-expert behavior and outputs executable joint or base commands without embodiment-specific controllers. Expected outcomes are improved zero-shot success rate and path efficiency on unseen physical robots and photorealistic environments compared to single-embodiment baselines and offline behavioral cloning, plus empirical characterization of how training population size and design choices affect generalization. Experiments: Datasets and environments: (1) Massive simulated training set of randomly generated robot embodiments: configurations for wheeled and 12-DOF quadrupeds sampled from parameter ranges (size, link masses, motor PD gains, friction); training pools of 128, 1024, and 4096 distinct embodiments. (2) Simulated photorealistic evaluation: four houses from Matterport3D with randomly sampled 20 start-goal pairs per house. (3) Challenging simulated terrains: stairs, rough height fields, randomized grids. (4) Real-world zero-shot evaluation: commercially available platforms not seen during training (examples: Clearpath Jackal, Clearpath Dingo, iRobot Create3, Unitree A1, Unitree Go2, ANYmal B, TurtleBot2). Baselines: ViNT (visual transformer waypoint generator with PD tracking), NavDP (visual diffusion waypoint generator with PD tracking), single-embodiment PPO expert deployed directly, MorAL + velocity-tracking controller for quadrupeds, offline behavioral cloning on aggregated expert dataset. Metrics: success rate (SR), success-weighted by inverse path length (SPL), normalized path length, collision rate (collisions per meter), mean action prediction error (MSE), smoothness (mean jerk), and sim-to-real performance drop. Training setup: Stage 1 experts trained with PPO using batch size 24576, parallel workers, network sizes (1024,512,256), curriculum over 384 subfields, domain randomization (friction, mass, sensor noise, motor delay). Train 5 expert policies covering small/large quadrupeds and wheeled templates for 4k epochs or until convergence. Stage 2 distillation: Nav-ACT transformer with 2 decoder layers, 4 heads, embedding size 256, sequence length S=6, chunk length 6, DAgger-style dataset aggregation; optimizer Adam, lr=1e-4, batch size 28672, 5000 iterations. Evaluation protocol: run 1000 trials per robot per method in MP3D; 500 trials per robot on challenging terrains; perform 20 real-world trials per robot per method with identical start-goal pairs; no fine-tuning during evaluation (zero-shot). Ablations: (A) training population size: 128 vs 1024 vs 4096; (B) loss: L2 vs L1 vs Huber; (C) imitation method: DAgger vs offline BC; (D) temporal ensemble: enabled vs disabled; (E) action chunk length: 1, 3, 6, 12; (F) privileged inputs ablation: remove proprioception or terrain height. Statistical analysis: report means and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; significance testing with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p<0.05. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sim-to-real mismatch: domain randomization may not cover real-world sensor failure modes, contact dynamics, or low-friction conditions, producing degraded real-world performance. Dynamics-generalization limits: randomized template range may not include extreme morphologies, high-DOF robots, or nonstandard actuators; policy may fail or produce unsafe commands outside training support. Safety and stability: direct low-level command outputs for quadrupeds can cause falls or hardware damage in edge cases due to unmodeled dynamics or delayed actuation. Data and evaluation bias: simulated obstacle sets and photorealistic houses may not represent all deployment scenarios, producing overly optimistic generalization metrics. Computational cost and scalability: training many expert policies and a large transformer requires substantial GPU resources and wall-clock time, limiting rapid iteration. Dependence on privileged expert quality: distilled policy quality is upper-bounded by expert policies; if experts exploit privileged sensors in ways not replicable from onboard inputs, distillation will fail. Hyperparameter sensitivity: performance may be sensitive to chunk length, transformer size, and DAgger schedule, requiring extensive tuning. Limited robot classes: current pipeline targets wheeled and 12-DOF quadrupeds; generalization to manipulators, bipeds, or substantially different DOF counts is not guaranteed.
